opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the first thing to realize is just how hopeless the problem looks if you take it at face value. If you have a vocabulary of tens of thousands of words and a sentence of, say, twenty or thirty tokens, the number of possible sequences is astronomically large, far larger than any training set could ever cover. So if a model had to learn the probability of whole sentences by memorizing them, it would be completely stuck. That's the curse of dimensionality in its purest form.

Next-token prediction helps in a first, almost trivial way: it factorizes the joint probability of a sentence into a product of conditional probabilities. Instead of modeling the whole object at once, you ask, given what came before, what comes next? But that alone doesn't solve the problem, because the context itself still lives in an enormous space. You still need to generalize to contexts you've never seen.

What I think really resolves it is structure in the data, and in particular hierarchical, compositional structure. Language isn't a random string of symbols. Words combine into phrases, phrases into clauses, clauses into sentences, a bit like a grammar. And crucially, many different low-level realizations mean the same higher-level thing. You have synonyms, different ways of saying the same phrase. If the model can learn that a group of tokens plays a given role regardless of exactly which tokens they are, it has effectively compressed the space. It no longer needs to see every combination, only enough to identify these latent variables.

In our work with simple generative models, like what we call the random hierarchy model, we can make this quantitative. The key point is that the latent structure leaves a statistical footprint: correlations between tokens and the next token, which decay with distance but remain detectable given enough data. As training data increases, the model can resolve correlations at larger and larger distances, which lets it build a deeper representation of the hierarchy. So you get a picture where the effective context the model can use grows with the number of training examples, and the sample complexity scales polynomially, not exponentially, in the relevant dimension.

So in a sense, next-token prediction works not because it's a magic objective, but because it's a natural way to exploit these local-to-global correlations. Each prediction is a local task, but solving it well forces the network to discover the hidden compositional variables. And that's also, I think, a nice way to understand why scaling laws look the way they do: more data unlocks progressively longer-range structure, layer by layer, and the test loss improves in steps that, averaged together, look like a smooth power law.

r001.rationale: The response says more data lets the model resolve longer-range correlations and build deeper representations, but does not describe coarser representations for distant content and finer ones near the predicted token.

r002.rationale: It links increasing data to progressively deeper representations and says the model can identify latent variables given enough data, conveying that abstract representations require substantial data.

r003.rationale: It describes grouping tokens that play the same role, but does not explain forming abstractions by grouping configurations that predict similar low-level surroundings.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is really the central puzzle, right? If you count the number of possible sentences, it grows exponentially with the length. So if you have a vocabulary of, say, tens of thousands of words, and sentences of a hundred tokens, the number of configurations is astronomically larger than anything you could ever see in a training set, even with trillions of tokens. So naively, learning seems impossible. You cannot memorize, you cannot interpolate in a sense that is meaningful in such a high-dimensional space. This is the curse of dimensionality.

So the way out, I think, is that language is not a random sequence of symbols. It has structure, and the key structure is that it is hierarchical and compositional. You have letters making words, words making phrases, phrases making sentences, and so on. At each level, you have a relatively small number of building blocks and a relatively small number of rules for how they combine. And crucially, the way a phrase can be built does not depend too much on what is happening very far away in the sentence. There is a kind of locality in the hierarchy.

Now, why does next-token prediction help with this? Because the task of predicting the next token forces you to learn the statistics of which words tend to appear in which context. And in a hierarchical grammar, two words that play the same role, let's say two synonyms, will tend to be followed by the same kinds of things. So by looking at the correlations between a token and its neighbors, you can effectively cluster tokens into groups that are interchangeable. Once you have done that, you have reduced the problem enormously, because now you don't need to see every sentence, you just need to see enough examples to figure out which words belong to the same category.

And then you can repeat this at the next level. Groups of tokens that behave similarly can be grouped into higher-level features, and so on. What we have shown in our work, with some synthetic models of hierarchical data, generative grammars essentially, is that a deep network trained on this kind of task learns exactly this structure, level by level. And you can compute how much data you need. It turns out the number of training examples scales polynomially with the size of the problem, not exponentially. So you beat the curse of dimensionality precisely because you exploit the compositional structure, and next-token prediction is a very natural objective for discovering that structure from correlations alone.

What I find quite remarkable is that the depth of the network matters a lot here. A shallow architecture cannot do this efficiently, because it would have to represent the whole mapping at once. A deep one can build the representation hierarchically, which mirrors the hierarchy of the data. So in a sense, the architecture and the data are matched, and that is why it works.

r001.rationale: The response describes hierarchical representations and local word correlations, but does not say that distant sentence content is represented coarsely and nearer content progressively more finely.

r002.rationale: It says the number of examples needed scales polynomially and that enough examples reveal word categories, but does not state that highly abstract next-token representations require large amounts of data.

r003.rationale: It says words that tend to be followed by the same kinds of things can be clustered as interchangeable, describing abstractions formed from items with similar predictive surroundings.

astra-6.text:
Well, you don’t try to estimate the probability of every possible sentence independently. You decompose it into the probability of each word given the words that came before. So the same model is reused at every step, and what it learns in one context can help it in another.

But that decomposition alone doesn’t solve the problem, because the number of possible contexts is also enormous. The essential thing is that language has structure. If the model can learn regularities shared across many contexts, it can predict sentences it has never encountered. So the question becomes: what structure does it learn, and how efficiently can it learn it from examples?

r001.rationale: It describes predicting each word from preceding words, but does not say representations of more distant content are coarser and nearer content progressively finer.

r002.rationale: It asks how efficiently structure can be learned from examples, but does not state that highly abstract representations require large amounts of data.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning regularities shared across contexts, but does not explain forming abstractions by grouping configurations with similar low-level surroundings.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the number of possible sentences is enormous, so you cannot learn by seeing every sentence. You have to exploit structure that is shared across sentences. Next-token prediction gives you a way to do that: you condition on the words you have already seen and learn a probability distribution for the next one. Repeating this lets you assign probabilities to entire sentences without enumerating them.

But the factorization itself doesn't solve the learning problem. The important question is whether the model discovers reusable structure—grammatical relationships, concepts, dependencies—that allows it to generalize to combinations it has never encountered. Predicting a token across many different contexts provides pressure to learn those regularities. So you're not memorizing all possible sentences; you're learning something about the process that generates them.

r001.rationale: It describes conditioning on prior words and predicting the next token, but not progressively coarser representations of distant content and finer ones near the predicted token.

r002.rationale: It mentions learning regularities across many contexts, but does not state that highly abstract representations require large amounts of data.

r003.rationale: It refers to discovering reusable structure, but does not explain forming abstractions by grouping configurations with similar low-level surroundings.
